title: Ham and Cheese Omelette
subtitle: A French omelette filled with cooked ham and melted cheddar
excerpt: Ham and cheese omelette is the filled version of a plain French omelette, the same technique, with cooked ham and cheddar laid across the centre just before rolling. The cheese melts from the heat of the egg alone.
sourceNotes: Ham and cheese is the most common filled omelette in French and British cafés. The technique is identical to a plain omelette, filling goes in just before rolling so the cheese melts without the egg overcooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Rolling the omelette over the filling in the pan, using a spatula to bring one edge over the centre, then tipping the pan to roll the omelette onto the plate with the seam underneath.

content.text: Ham and cheese omelette is a filled French omelette, the egg technique is the same, but the filling goes in at the last moment so the cheddar melts from the residual heat of the egg rather than cooking on the hob. The result is a pale, soft omelette with a warm, slightly runny cheese centre and pieces of cooked ham distributed through it. It is a fast, satisfying breakfast that rewards having your filling prepared before the eggs ever touch the pan.

items.prepNote: cooked and roughly chopped, or substitute cooked ham

content.text: Grate the {{cheddar}} cheddar and chop the {{back-bacon}} cooked ham or bacon into small pieces. Have both ready beside the hob before you start the omelette. A filled omelette gives you no time to grate cheese mid-cook, the egg will be done and starting to overbrown while you are still at the grater. Cooked ham is the traditional filling; leftover cooked back bacon works equally well and adds a smoky flavour that pairs well with cheddar.

Beat the {{eggs}} eggs well with a fork, season with a pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes and {{black-pepper}} black pepper. Heat a 20 cm non-stick pan over medium-high heat for a full minute, then add the {{unsalted-butter}} butter and let it foam and begin to subside. Pour in the egg mixture and immediately start shaking the pan and drawing a silicone spatula across the base in short strokes. After twenty to twenty-five seconds the egg will be almost set with a thin wet layer on top. Stop moving it.

Scatter the ham and two-thirds of the grated cheddar across the centre of the omelette, a strip running from edge to edge rather than one clump in the middle, so the filling distributes when the omelette is

. Tilt the pan away from you and use the spatula to fold the near third of the egg over the filling, then roll the omelette onto a warm plate, seam-side down. Scatter the remaining cheese over the top, it will begin to melt from the heat of the omelette. Serve immediately.

Mature cheddar is the standard choice and melts readily into the warm egg. Gruyère is the French alternative, it has a nuttier, more complex flavour and melts even more smoothly. A mix of the two is particularly good. Whatever cheese you use, grate it coarsely rather than finely, fine cheese tends to clump and melt unevenly, while coarser pieces melt into distinct pools inside the omelette.

Filling is cold inside when omelette is ready: the ham and cheese were fridge-cold when they went in. Bring them to room temperature, or warm the ham briefly in the microwave before scattering it over.
Omelette tears when rolling: either the egg was overcooked before folding, or there was too much filling. The filling should cover no more than the middle third of the omelette, not be piled high.

Cheese has not melted when omelette hits the plate: the omelette was slightly undercooked at the fold stage, so there was not enough residual heat. Add an extra few seconds of cooking before you scatter the filling in.
